### Enhanced Information Summary

The primary immune cells capable of killing tumor cells with decreased MHC class I expression are natural killer (NK) cells. This is supported by the understanding that MHC class I molecules typically help cytotoxic T-cells recognize and eliminate cells. However, cancer cells often evade this immune surveillance by downregulating MHC class I molecules. NK cells are uniquely adapted to recognize and kill cells that have low levels of MHC class I expression, a mechanism known as "missing self" recognition.

The reasoning chains for natural killer cells correctly identify that decreased MHC class I expression leads to reduced effectiveness of cytotoxic T-cells and increased activation of NK cells. NK cells detect these abnormalities and can induce apoptosis in the tumor cells. This aligns well with the standard immunological consensus and is supported by evidence paths showing interactions between NK cells and unspecified tumor cells, as well as the interaction between NK cells and the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC).

Other immune cells like macrophages, B-cells, and eosinophils are less effective in this specific context. Macrophages can recognize and phagocytize tumor cells, but they do not specifically target cells based on MHC class I expression levels. B-cells produce antibodies and are not directly involved in killing cells with low MHC class I expression. Eosinophils primarily target parasites and are not effective against tumor cells in this scenario.

In conclusion, the most capable immune cells for killing tumor cells with decreased MHC class I expression in this patient are natural killer cells, due to their ability to recognize and respond to the lack of MHC class I molecules on the surface of these cells.
